summary: Shared REST Hyper loopback runtime adapter for messenger, mail, social, and community route catalogs.
claim_boundary: This slice proves local REST runtime composition only: all four framework-free REST route catalogs can be registered into the canonical Hyper adapter, and local TCP loopback reaches probe plus contract-only routes. It adds a scoped Tokio dependency-rationale allowance for this runtime adapter only. It does not claim production Gateway/TLS rollout, DNS, ArgoCD sync, branch protection, live service deployment, or generic JSON write-body execution for typed write routes.

best_practice_research.used_for: Confirmed the accept-loop pattern using tokio TcpListener, TokioIo, service_fn, and serving connections on spawned Tokio tasks.

best_practice_research.source_quality: official docs.rs API docs for hyper-util 0.1 auto connection builder
best_practice_research.used_for: Confirmed the existing adapter's ConnBuilder::serve_connection boundary remains the correct Hyper-family concentration point.

source_basis.use: Messenger OpenAPI route catalog and probe/contract-only dispatch semantics.
Mail OpenAPI route catalog and readiness/liveness dispatch semantics.
Social OpenAPI route catalog and typed write-plan route classification.
Community route catalog, including three typed write-plan route seams.
Canonical Hyper import boundary and secure request body/header handling.

findings: The Hyper adapter gained only a listener-bound entrypoint; the accept/serve loop remains single-sourced and serve(addr, ...) delegates to it.
The new shared REST adapter is a small catalog-to-router binder rather than four duplicated per-service runtime crates.
Every messenger, mail, social, and community REST catalog route is registered into a Hyper-compatible router, giving later cell binaries a deterministic composition seam.
Backbone GitHub Actions and Jenkins matrices now include the shared REST runtime adapter in each microservice lane.
Tests assert honest route classification counts for all four services: probe, contract-only, and typed-write-plan-required routes are distinct.
A local TCP loopback test reaches all four REST service catalogs through Hyper for /health and representative contract-only routes.
Typed write routes intentionally return a 501 typed_write_plan_required response instead of faking JSON-body execution.
F3_adversarial.not_applicable_reason: This is a new runtime seam rather than a defect fix; adversarial coverage targets false runtime/live claims and missing route registration.
F3_adversarial.diagnostic_asserted: HTTP/1.1 200 for /health and HTTP/1.1 501 contract_only for one contract route per service over local TCP.

findings: Future per-cell binaries can call build_backbone_rest_router or serve_backbone_rest_microservice_listener with a service enum and readiness dependency list.
The shared BackboneRestReadinessDependency avoids exposing four service-specific readiness structs at the runtime composition boundary.
Focused cargo check, unit tests, clippy -D warnings, fmt, and a workflow governance-smoke command passed for the new runtime seam.
The route catalog test hard-codes expected counts so route drift in any service surfaces as a failing test.
Chose one shared REST runtime adapter over per-service runtime crates to keep catalog binding policy centralized.
Chose raw local TCP test clients over adding a Hyper client dependency path, preserving the existing rule that Hyper-family imports stay in the canonical adapter crate.
alternatives_named: Add one runtime crate per service
Add Hyper client usage to the test adapter
Keep only framework-free direct dispatch tests without a socket
F6_alternatives.selected_rationale: The selected path proves real local TCP/Hyper routing while minimizing dependency surface and avoiding false JSON write-body claims.
rejected_reasons: Per-service runtime crates would duplicate route classification and readiness mapping.
A Hyper client would expand the Hyper dependency surface outside the existing server adapter boundary.
Direct dispatch alone would not reduce the local runtime-loopback evidence gap.

findings: No secrets, credentials, tenant records, production endpoints, DNS records, cert material, or provider credentials were added.
The adapter preserves the existing Hyper runtime body cap and header validation boundary by reusing oya-http-runtime-hyper-adapter dispatch and serve_listener.
Responses are static JSON-shaped metadata for probes/route state and do not echo request bodies or tenant data.
Route registration happens at composition/build time; per-request handling performs a router match plus a small static response for probe/contract-only paths.
No database, broker, JSON parser, or external network call is introduced in the local REST runtime adapter.
The adapter's non-claim text, task plan, catalog row, and evidence distinguish local runtime proof from live compliance/control operation evidence.
Reverting removes one new workspace crate, one catalog row, CI matrix entries, the listener-bound helper, and task/evidence text without altering service business logic or schemas.
The response body includes low-cardinality service/method/path/runtime_handler fields suitable for later loopback smoke assertions; it does not claim production telemetry.
Existing serve(addr, ...) behavior remains source-compatible and delegates to the new serve_listener helper.
The crate name follows the existing shared backbone adapter pattern: oya-shared-backbone-rest-runtime-adapter.
tasks/plan.md, tasks/todo.md, catalog metadata, and multispectrum evidence document scope, verification, and non-claims.
The Hyper-family import boundary remains in oya-http-runtime-hyper-adapter; the shared REST runtime adapter consumes only the canonical adapter API plus framework-free route catalogs.

The new crate is cataloged as a shared runtime adapter and depends outward on REST composition surfaces plus inward HTTP router/middleware kernels, matching existing architecture-boundaries allowances.
No third-party dependency was added; the crate uses existing workspace dependencies and path crates.
Runtime route classification is derived directly from existing OpenAPI route catalogs and service-owned RouteHandlerStatus values.
Backbone CI path filters, package matrices, Jenkins package lists, and governance smoke were updated to include the shared REST runtime adapter.
